title: Simultaneously Query-Optimal Quantum Linear-System Algorithm
authors: Minbo Gao, Zhengfeng Ji, Chenghua Liu
abstract: Quantum linear-system algorithms access the coefficient matrix through a block-encoding oracle $U_A$ and the right-hand side through a state-preparation oracle $U_b$. The optimal query complexities of these two oracles are known separately: $O(κ\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries to $U_A$ and $O(κ/s)$ queries to $U_b$, where $s=α\|A^{-1}b\|$. Whether a single algorithm can achieve both bounds simultaneously has remained open.   We resolve this question affirmatively. Given a constant-factor estimate of $s$, we give a quantum linear-system algorithm that prepares the normalized solution to error $\varepsilon$ using simultaneously $ O\left(κ\log\frac1\varepsilon\right)$ queries to $U_A$ and $O\left(κ/{s}\right)$ queries to $U_b$. The algorithm separates state preparation from precision refinement, so only the matrix-query count depends on the target accuracy.   We also prove a matching same-instance worst-case lower bound: for every quantum linear-system algorithm and every solution-norm scale, there exists a single Hermitian instance on which that algorithm requires both $Ω(κ\log(1/\varepsilon))$ matrix queries and $Ω(κ/s)$ state-preparation queries. Thus the two oracle complexities can be optimized simultaneously, and the resulting bounds are jointly optimal.
summary: This paper solves the open problem of simultaneously optimizing query complexity for the Quantum Linear-System Problem (QLS). It presents an algorithm that achieves optimal query bounds for both the matrix and vector oracles, matched by a rigorous lower bound proof. This result is crucial for understanding the fundamental resource requirements of quantum algorithms solving linear equations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the quantum linear-system problem (QLS), which requires preparing a quantum state proportional to the solution $A^{-1}b$ given quantum access to the matrix $A$ and vector $b$. The core challenge is achieving optimal query complexity simultaneously for both the matrix and vector oracles.
main_result: The authors provide a quantum algorithm that achieves simultaneous query-optimality, requiring $O(\kappa \log(1/\epsilon))$ queries to the matrix oracle $U_A$ and $O(\kappa/s)$ queries to the state-preparation oracle $U_b$. This is matched by a proven lower bound.
method: The algorithm employs a multi-stage process that separates state preparation from precision refinement, utilizing canonical transducers. The lower bound is established via a one-sided hybrid argument on a single Hermitian instance.
model_or_system: The problem is analyzed in the standard block-encoding model for quantum linear systems, where the input is defined by quantum access to the coefficient matrix $A$ and the right-hand side vector $b$.
key_observables: The primary observables are the query complexities for the two oracles: $O(\kappa \log(1/\epsilon))$ for $U_A$ and $O(\kappa/s)$ for $U_b$.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the condition number $\kappa$, the target error $\epsilon$, and the solution norm scale $s = \alpha\|A^{-1}b\|$.
main_assumptions: The algorithm assumes the availability of a constant-factor estimate $s$ of the solution norm scale. The lower bound relies on constructing a single Hermitian instance that is hard for both query types.
figures_summary: The notes mention Table 1 comparing upper bounds and Table 2 comparing lower bounds, both highlighting the simultaneous optimality achieved by the presented work.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the QLS problem, reviews known separate bounds, and then presents the main algorithm achieving simultaneous optimality. It concludes with a matching lower bound proof, detailing the separation of state preparation and precision refinement.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a concrete, provably optimal quantum algorithm for a fundamental problem in quantum computation, directly impacting the theoretical limits of quantum simulation and quantum machine learning algorithms.
